title: Century‐Long Butterfly Redistribution Reshapes Assemblage Trait–Temperature Relationships Across Fennoscandia
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

To test whether assemblage trait–environment relationships remain stationary during long-term species redistribution, focusing on colour, wing size and thermal affinity.

Location

Sweden and Finland (50 biogeographic provinces).

Time Period

1900–2025.

Major Taxa Studied

Butterflies (Papilionoidea; 134 species, including 120 with colour data).

Methods

We reconstructed cumulative provincial assemblages at five time points from first-record data and calculated unweighted community means of male and female CIELAB colour (lightness L*, green–red a*, blue–yellow b*), wing size and species temperature index. Mixed-effects models were used to test whether relationships with long-term baseline temperature varied among time points while accounting for shorter-term temperature anomalies. Spatial sensitivity models and contemporary GBIF assemblages were used to evaluate sensitivity to spatial dependence and cumulative recording.

Results

The relationship between assemblage lightness and temperature changed strongly through time in both sexes of butterfly species. The historical association of colder provinces with darker assemblages weakened in both sexes. The contemporary male gradient was negative in the primary mixed-effects model, but its uncertainty increased under spatial and recording-window sensitivity analyses; the female gradient did not differ from zero. Year × temperature interactions were significant for all seven colour and size responses (all p < 0.001), whereas period-window temperature anomalies explained little variation. Community thermal affinity increased and changed in parallel with lightness, and temporal restructuring persisted under non-cumulative GBIF endpoints and removal of presences lacking recent records.

Main Conclusions

Trait–environment relationships can become restructured as regional species pools are reassembled. Composition-based trait gradients should therefore be treated as dynamic outcomes of ecological filtering rather than stationary rules. Because historical assemblages were reconstructed cumulatively, the results concern colonisation-driven community reassembly rather than local extirpation or within-species adaptation.
